\title{Two-Field Physics Is Enough to Represent One-Dimensional LTE Stellar Atmospheres: Learned and Emulator-Independent Initialization}
\titlerunning{Two-field stellar-atmosphere initialization}

\author{Jiadong Li\inst{1}, Yuan-Sen Ting\inst{1,2}}
\authorrunning{J. Li \& Y.-S. Ting}

\institute{Max Planck Institute for Astronomy\\
  \email{jdli@mpia.de}}


\date{Received ---; accepted ---}

\abstract
{A one-dimensional LTE stellar atmosphere is commonly initialized through six
depth-dependent fields. Four of these fields, however, are constrained by the
equation of state, opacity, radiative transfer, and hydrostatic equilibrium
once the column mass $m(\tau)$ and temperature $T(\tau)$ are specified. We
separate the sufficiency of this two-field representation from the harder
problem of predicting a useful initial state. Reconstructing the four
dependent fields from exact converged $(m,T)$ profiles preserves both the
atmospheric structure and the emergent spectrum. On a 60-star development
sample, a learned two-field initializer reduces the mean iteration count from
\NprodIterMean\ to \NlearnedIterMean. An independent 200-star test confirms this
computational advantage, but also shows larger tail errors in the predicted
profiles and spectra and a slightly lower fraction of usable atmospheres than
the six-field initializer. We further construct a hydrostatic
grey--convective initializer directly from stellar labels, without an
atmosphere emulator. Most development stars converge from this physical
approximation, but successful calculations require
\NphysicalDevIterMean\ iterations on average, substantially more than for the
learned start. A subsequent comparison on the same 200 stars shows the same
accuracy--cost trade-off. In a separate \NMstarCases-node, solar-composition
MARCS experiment below 4000 K, a temperature sequence reaches a
\NMstarDwarfCoolestContinuation\,K dwarf missed by direct initialization, but
its \NMstarDwarfFluxCoolest\% all-layer flux imbalance shows that formal
convergence does not yet establish a physically acceptable cool atmosphere.
Thus $(m,T)$ is sufficient as a physical representation. Learned predictions
reach the convergence basin efficiently but are not yet robust across the
sampled label range, whereas the emulator-independent construction is
physically informative but slower and less reliable.}

\keywords{stars: atmospheres --
  methods: numerical --
  radiative transfer --
  techniques: spectroscopic --
  stars: late-type --
  stars: fundamental parameters}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Large spectroscopic surveys usually rely on grids of precomputed stellar
atmospheres, such as ATLAS \citep{kurucz1970, castelli2003}, MARCS
\citep{gustafsson2008}, or PHOENIX
\citep{hauschildt1999, husser2013}. Interpolation within such grids is fast,
but its accuracy depends on the density and geometry of the grid
\citep{meszaros2013}. Payne Zero \citep[hereafter Paper~I]{ting2026} instead
accelerates the underlying Kurucz calculation, making it feasible to compute
an atmosphere for each set of stellar labels. In this regime, the
number of iterations needed for convergence becomes an important part of the
computational cost.

The iteration count depends on the initial atmospheric structure. Paper~I
uses a neural network to predict this structure from the stellar labels.
However, a model atmosphere is not an arbitrary collection of profiles. At
each of \NgridLayers\ depth points, the solver stores column mass $m$,
temperature $T$, gas pressure $P_{\rm gas}$, electron density $n_{\rm e}$,
Rosseland mean opacity $\kappa_{\rm R}$, and radiative acceleration
$g_{\rm rad}$. Once the stellar labels and the profiles $m(\tau)$ and
$T(\tau)$ are specified, the equation of state, opacity calculation,
radiative transfer, and hydrostatic equilibrium constrain the remaining four
fields. Predicting all six profiles independently can therefore introduce
combinations that are individually plausible but mutually inconsistent.

This observation motivates a reduced representation in which only
$m(\tau)$ and $T(\tau)$ are supplied. The remaining fields are reconstructed
with the atmosphere solver's own microphysics while the two supplied
profiles are held fixed. The closure is iterated to self-consistency before
the ordinary temperature correction begins. We distinguish the
\emph{two-field representation}, which is the pair $(m,T)$, from the
\emph{two-field physical initializer}, which also includes this
self-consistent reconstruction and the subsequent atmosphere iteration. The
distinction is important: a representation may be sufficient even when an
approximate predictor does not place every star within the convergence basin.

The same representation also allows a complementary physical construction.
We derive $m(\tau)$ and $T(\tau)$ from an Eddington-grey atmosphere,
hydrostatic equilibrium, approximate Rosseland opacity, and a Saha-aware
convective adjustment. This initializer contains no fitted atmospheric
profiles and is independent of the neural atmosphere emulator. Its
convergence therefore tests whether the
solver can be initialized from a compact physical approximation rather than
from an interpolated or learned atmosphere.

Cool M-star atmospheres provide a stringent boundary test because molecular
equilibrium, opacity, and convection strongly shape their thermal structure
\citep{gustafsson2008,husser2013}. The two-field representation also suggests
a physical continuation experiment: a converged warmer atmosphere can supply
$(m,T)$ for a nearby effective temperature, after which the dependent fields
are reconstructed before the next solve. This tests whether neighbouring cool
atmospheres occupy a connected solution branch; it does not extrapolate the
learned initializer beyond its training support.

Several lines of related work approach this construction without coinciding
with it. Interpolation of precomputed atmosphere grids is the classical way
to avoid the cost of a solve, and its error budget in spectra and structure
is well characterized \citep{meszaros2013}; more recently, neural
interpolation of complete atmosphere structures between grid points reaches
high accuracy in the grid's interior \citep[][iNNterpol]{westendorp2023},
and spectral-level neural emulation of the mapping from labels to spectra
underlies The Payne \citep{ting2019}, on which the fitting side of Paper~I
builds. Physics-constrained neural surrogates of the atmosphere structure
itself, with the governing equations entering the loss, have also been
demonstrated \citep[][Kurucz-a1, an arXiv preprint and workshop
paper]{li2025kurucza1}. All of these approaches replace or sidestep the
solver, whereas here the prediction is used only to start the original solver
and is assessed through the subsequent convergence trajectory and final
atmosphere.

We address four questions. First, do exact converged $(m,T)$ profiles retain
enough information to reconstruct the full atmosphere and its spectrum?
Second, can a neural predictor of these two profiles reduce the cost of
convergence without compromising the final atmosphere? Third, can an
emulator-independent physical approximation reach the same convergence
basin? Fourth, can temperature continuation in the reduced coordinates reach
selected M-star atmospheres below the 4000 K corpus boundary, and are those
atmospheres in flux balance? We separate the representation test from the two
initialization tests, and we assess the learned initializer on an independent
200-star sample that was not used during model development.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:solver}
gives the minimal solver description needed to define the reduced state, and
Sect.~\ref{sec:reduced} defines the physical reconstruction.
Section~\ref{sec:data} describes the evaluation design.
Section~\ref{sec:results} tests representation sufficiency, compares the
learned two-field initializer with the six-field reference, evaluates the
grey--convective construction, examines the cool M-star boundary, and reports
the independent learned test and post-hoc physical comparison. Additional
solver diagnostics, the fitted analytic initializer, and reproducibility
information are collected in the appendices.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\section{Atmosphere solver}
\label{sec:solver}

\subsection{Atmospheric state and physical closure}
\label{sec:state}

The reference solver computes a plane-parallel, hydrostatic, one-dimensional
LTE atmosphere on a fixed Rosseland optical-depth grid,
\begin{equation}
  \tau_{\rm std}(i) = 10^{-6.875 + 0.125\,i}, \qquad
  i=0,\ldots,\NgridLayers-1.
  \label{eq:grid}
\end{equation}
It stores six depth-dependent profiles,
\begin{equation}
  \mathbf{p} =
  \bigl\{m_j,T_j,P_{{\rm gas},j},n_{{\rm e},j},
  \kappa_{{\rm R},j},g_{{\rm rad},j}\bigr\}_{j=1}^{\NgridLayers},
  \label{eq:state}
\end{equation}
namely column mass, temperature, gas pressure, electron density, Rosseland
mean opacity and radiative acceleration. Additional numerical variables and
frequency-dependent opacities are retained during iteration but are not part
of this six-profile representation.

The closure couples these fields through the equation of state, opacity and
radiative transfer. In particular,
\begin{align}
  g_{\rm rad}(m) &= \frac{1}{c}\int_0^\infty \chi_\nu F_\nu\,{\rm d}\nu,
  \qquad
  P_{\rm rad}(m) = \int_0^m g_{\rm rad}(m')\,{\rm d}m', \label{eq:grad}\\
  P_{\rm gas} &= g\,m-P_{\rm rad}. \label{eq:hse}
\end{align}
Here $\chi_\nu$ is the total extinction per unit mass and $F_\nu$ is the
monochromatic flux. Turbulent pressure is neglected, while microturbulence
enters the opacity calculation as a line-broadening parameter. At fixed
labels and fixed $(m,T)$, the equation of state, opacity and transfer routines
therefore determine the other four stored fields. This physical closure is the
reason a six-field initializer can contain mutually inconsistent quantities.

\subsection{Energy balance}
\label{sec:correction}

The ordinary solver does more than synchronize the closure: it changes $T$ and
$m$ until the total flux is constant,
\begin{equation}
  F_{\rm rad}(m)+F_{\rm conv}(m)=\sigma T_{\rm eff}^{4},
  \qquad
  \epsilon_F =
  \frac{F_{\rm rad}+F_{\rm conv}}{\sigma T_{\rm eff}^{4}}-1.
  \label{eq:energy}
\end{equation}
We use the temperature correction and damping scheme of Paper~I without
modification. Each correction also remaps the column-mass coordinate.
Consequently, inconsistencies among the initial profiles can alter both
$T(\tau)$ and $m(\tau)$ during the first iteration.

\subsection{Fixed-point iteration}
\label{sec:map}

Writing $\mathbf{x}$ for the complete atmospheric state, one iteration can be
summarized as
\begin{equation}
  \begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{x}^{(n)}
  &\longrightarrow
  \bigl(P_{\rm gas},n_{\rm e},\chi_\nu\bigr)^{(n)}
  \longrightarrow
  \bigl(g_{\rm rad},\kappa_{\rm R},F_{\rm conv}\bigr)^{(n)} \\
  &\longrightarrow
  (T,m)^{(n+1)}
  \xrightarrow{\rm remap}
  \mathbf{x}^{(n+1)} ,
  \end{aligned}
  \label{eq:pass}
\end{equation}
or $\mathbf{x}^{(n+1)}=\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{x}^{(n)})$. The converged atmosphere
is the fixed point of this map. Convergence is declared from the deep-layer
temperature change,
\begin{equation}
  \epsilon_T =
  \max_{j\in{\rm deep}}
  \left|\frac{T_j^{(n+1)}-T_j^{(n)}}{T_j^{(n+1)}}\right|
  <5\times10^{-4},
  \label{eq:stop}
\end{equation}
with a minimum of three iterations. All calculations use the convergence
criterion and iteration scheme described in Paper~I.
\section{Two-field physical representation}
\label{sec:reduced}

\subsection{Choice of independent profiles}

We use $(m,T)$ as the two independent depth-dependent coordinates and treat
the remaining fields as functionals of those coordinates, the stellar labels
and the fixed depth grid:
\begin{equation}
  \bigl(P_{\rm gas}, n_{\rm e}, \kappa_{\rm R}, g_{\rm rad}\bigr)
  = \mathcal{F}\bigl[m(\tau), T(\tau); \theta\bigr],
  \label{eq:reduced}
\end{equation}
where $\theta$ denotes the stellar labels. The operator $\mathcal{F}$ consists
of the same equation of state, opacity calculation, radiative transfer, and
hydrostatic closure used during the atmosphere iteration, but is evaluated
without changing $m$ or $T$. Thus two independent profiles determine the four
remaining profiles through the physical closure. The six stored profiles
therefore occupy a constrained functional subspace parameterized by two
depth-dependent functions, rather than six independently variable functions.

Figure~\ref{fig:state} compares three ways to initialize the same solver. The
six-field neural initializer predicts all six stored fields. The learned
two-field initializer predicts only $(m,T)$ and synchronizes the four
dependent fields at fixed coordinates. The hydrostatic grey--convective
initializer instead constructs $m$, $T$, and an approximate Rosseland opacity
directly from the stellar labels. All three initial states then enter the same
atmosphere iteration.

\begin{figure*}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\hsize]{fig_state.pdf}
  \caption{Three initialization paths for the same atmosphere solver.
    \emph{(a)} The six-field network predicts all six stored fields directly.
    \emph{(b)} The two-field network predicts only $m(\tau)$ and $T(\tau)$.
    At fixed $(m,T)$, the equation of state, opacity, radiative
    transfer and hydrostatic closure are repeated until the pressure is
    self-consistent. \emph{(c)} The emulator-independent construction retains
    the grey-atmosphere column mass, applies a convective temperature
    adjustment, and evaluates the opacity at
    $(T_{\rm conv},P=g\,m_{\rm grey})$. The temperature adjustment does not
    trigger a second integration of the column-mass coordinate. All three
    paths use the same stellar labels, depth grid, solver, and convergence
    criterion.}
  \label{fig:state}
\end{figure*}

\subsection{Synchronization to self-consistency}
\label{sec:consistency}

One evaluation of $\mathcal{F}$ is insufficient. The populations and opacities
are evaluated at the input gas pressure, while the transfer solution changes
the radiation pressure and hence the gas pressure implied by
Eq.~(\ref{eq:hse}). If the energy iteration starts immediately, its first
temperature correction acts on that inconsistency. Even when the exact
converged $(m,T)$ profiles are supplied, a single closure evaluation therefore
changes the uppermost column-mass layers.

The inconsistency is largest at the top boundary, where optical depth is
initialized by
\begin{equation}
  \tau_{0} = \kappa_{0}\,m_{0},
  \label{eq:seed}
\end{equation}
which assumes constant opacity above the first grid point. This approximation
localizes the largest residual to the surface layers. Repeating the closure
reduces the residual substantially, whereas modifying the initial radiation
pressure alone does not.

We therefore hold $m$ and $T$ fixed, repeat the four physical stages,
and monitor the largest pass-to-pass change in $\log_{10}P_{\rm gas}$. The
exact-coordinate calculations use \NsyncPasses\ passes. The learned
initializer stops below \NsyncPressureTolerance\,dex, with at most
\NsyncMaxPasses\ passes. Cases that do not reach this tolerance do not proceed
to the atmosphere iteration and are reported as reconstruction failures. The
four dependent fields are evaluated before any temperature
correction or remapping. Appendix~\ref{app:resolution} tests the remaining
grid and top-boundary limitations.

\section{Atmosphere sample and evaluation}
\label{sec:data}

\subsection{Atmosphere sample and data splits}

All experiments draw on \NcorpusStars\ converged atmosphere models on the
grid of Eq.~(\ref{eq:grid}). The five-label support spans
$4000$--$10\,500$\,K in effective temperature, $0.7$--$5.3$ in $\log g$,
$-2.5$ to $+0.5$ in $[\rm M/H]$, $-0.1$ to $+0.5$ in
$[\alpha/\rm M]$, and $0.5$--$4.0$\,km\,s$^{-1}$ in microturbulence.
The learned model is trained on the corpus training split and assessed on a
60-star development sample excluded from training and validation. A separate
200-star test sample is disjoint from all training, validation, and
development rows. It was selected before the final model was evaluated and is
an independent test for the learned initializer. The same 200 stars had
already been examined before the hydrostatic grey--convective initializer was
introduced. Their subsequent use for that method is therefore a post-hoc
comparison rather than independent evidence.

The corpus contains only atmospheres that converged in fewer than thirty
iterations. Every convergence claim is therefore conditional on the region
already represented by this corpus; the experiments do not test whether a new
initializer rescues labels for which the solver fails from the outset.

A separate cool-star boundary sample is not drawn from this corpus. It consists
of \NMstarCases\ native MARCS atmospheres at solar composition:
\NMstarDwarfCases\ dwarfs with $\log g=5.0$ and
$\xi=1$\,km\,s$^{-1}$, and \NMstarGiantCases\ giants with
$\log g=1.5$ and $\xi=2$\,km\,s$^{-1}$. Each gravity sequence contains
$T_{\rm eff}=3000$, 3300, 3500, and 3750\,K. This sparse grid is designed to
contrast high- and low-gravity atmospheres below the 4000\,K corpus boundary;
it is not a representative sample of the M-star population.

\subsection{Initialization methods}

We compare three classes of initialization. The Paper~I reference model
predicts all six profiles directly. The learned two-field model predicts only
$(m,T)$ and obtains the remaining profiles from the physical reconstruction
of Sect.~\ref{sec:reduced}. Its final configuration was selected using the
development sample before it was applied to the independent test sample. The
grey--convective initializer supplies $(m,T,\kappa_{\rm R})$ from physical
approximations with no fitted atmospheric profiles. It is evaluated first on
the development sample and then, without changing the construction or
numerical limits, on the same 200-star sample. A compact fitted
analytic approximation is included as an additional comparison in
Appendix~\ref{app:analytic}.

For the learned two-field model, reconstruction begins from the stellar labels
and $P_{\rm gas}=gm$; no predicted field from the six-field model is used.
This independence applies to inference, not to training: the target
$(m,T)$ profiles come from converged full atmospheres. The synchronization
criterion is defined through gas pressure, so the dependent fields are
self-consistent only to the stated numerical tolerance.

For the physical experiment, the grey, coupled convective, and
grey--convective initializers are compared on the same 60 stars. Each
calculation is followed for at most \NvfourPolicyIterationLimit\ iterations
and \NvfourPolicyTimeoutSeconds\,s. These common limits define the reported
non-convergences and timeouts. The comparison isolates the effect of retaining
the grey column mass when the temperature profile is adjusted for convection.

For the cool-star experiment, each MARCS node is first tested by supplying its
native $(m,T)$ profiles directly to the Payne Zero physical closure. A second
calculation begins at 4000\,K and proceeds through
$3750\rightarrow3500\rightarrow3300\rightarrow3000$\,K. Only $(m,T)$ is
transferred between neighbouring temperatures; the dependent fields are
reconstructed at every step. Both calculations use the unchanged convergence
criterion and a 30-iteration limit. Carrying the full atmospheric state between
steps is retained only as a control and does not determine the reported
atmospheres.

\subsection{Performance measures}

We quantify performance at three levels. Profile accuracy is measured against
the converged atmosphere. Numerical behavior is characterized by the
convergence fraction, iteration count, residual contraction, and frequency of
non-monotonic trajectories. Finally, converged spectra are compared over
\NgateWindowLo--\NgateWindowHi\,nm at $R=\NgateResolution$. We retain
\NgateBar\ as a common reference level across the experiments. The reference
solver can itself exceed this value when restarted from a different converged
state, so crossing it is reported as a discrepancy rather than treated as
a universal pass--fail boundary. Appendix~\ref{app:gates} gives the complete
definitions.

For the M-star boundary sample, no spectrum is yet available. We therefore
report the maximum absolute relative flux error over all depth layers at the
final solver iteration. This quantity tests flux balance independently of the
temperature-based stopping rule; no post-hoc flux threshold is imposed.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

The representation and initialization experiments use the
\NevalStars-star development sample. The independent learned test and the
post-hoc physical comparison use the same 200 stars, with the different
interpretations established in Sect.~\ref{sec:data}.

\subsection{Representation sufficiency}
\label{sec:sufficiency}

We first isolate the representation from any prediction error. For each
evaluation star, we retain the converged $(m,T)$ profiles, discard the other
four fields, and reconstruct them through $\mathcal{F}$.

Figure~\ref{fig:reconstruction} gives the resulting comparison. The four
rebuilt fields agree with the values to which the solver itself converged at
$10^{-3}$ or better in the median. Across the four fields, the pointwise
$p_{90}$ errors range from \NreconPninetyLow\ to
\NreconPninetyHigh. The largest individual errors,
\NreconMaximumLow--\NreconMaximumHigh, are confined to the extreme upper and
lower boundary layers.

We next restart the solver from the reconstructed atmosphere and, as a
reference, from the original six-field converged state. Both initializations
converge for all stars. The
reconstructed states require \NoracleIterMean\ iterations on average,
compared with \NsixIterMean\ for the six-field states.
\NoracleAtFloor\ of \NevalStars\ reconstructed atmospheres reach the
three-iteration minimum, compared with \NsixAtFloor\ for the reference.
Only \NoracleGapStars\ stars differ in iteration count, by no more than
\NoracleGapMax\ iterations.

Because most stars reach the minimum number of iterations, the small
difference between \NoracleIterMean\ and \NsixIterMean\ is not a meaningful
measure of convergence speed. Both initial states also begin at a
first-iteration residual of about \NoracleFirstResidual, already inside the
$5\times10^{-4}$ convergence threshold. Their contraction ratios and
non-monotonic fractions therefore characterize numerical fluctuations near
the fixed point and are not directly comparable to initializations that begin
farther from convergence.

We finally test whether the reconstructed state changes the emergent
spectrum. Comparing the converged spectra obtained from the reconstructed and
six-field states over \NgateWindowLo--\NgateWindowHi\,nm, we find that
the normalized flux differs by a median of \NtruthGateMedian, with a maximum
of \NtruthGateMax\ and \NtruthGateOver\ of \NtruthGateStars\ stars above
the common reference level; the median is roughly \NtruthGateFactor\ times
smaller than that level. Total flux and continuum behave in the same way
(Table~\ref{tab:spectral}, first row). Figure~\ref{fig:representation-spectra}
shows this comparison directly across the label support, including the star
with the largest normalized-flux difference. Within the tested parameter and
wavelength ranges, the four dependent fields can therefore be reconstructed
from $(m,T)$ without a measurable change in the emergent spectrum.

    representation test. The black curves start from the reference six-field atmosphere;
    the orange curves start after discarding four fields and rebuilding them

% The grid and top-boundary controls are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:resolution};
% they are diagnostic limits rather than a separate main-text result.

\subsection{Temperature continuation into the M-star regime}
\label{sec:mstar}

Within this sparse grid, direct starts show a clear gravity dependence
(Fig.~\ref{fig:mstar-solver} and Table~\ref{tab:mstar}). All
\NMstarGiantDirectConverged\ of \NMstarGiantCases\ M-giant atmospheres satisfy
the unchanged temperature criterion, whereas only
\NMstarDwarfDirectConverged\ of \NMstarDwarfCases\ M-dwarf atmospheres does so.
The successful dwarf is the warmest node, at 3750\,K.

Temperature continuation changes the numerical boundary for the dwarfs. It
reaches the \NMstarDwarfCoolestContinuation\,K dwarf after the direct start at
the same temperature has exhausted the iteration limit. The sequence then
fails at 3300\,K and therefore does not reach 3000\,K. For the giants,
continuation reaches 3750 and 3500\,K but fails at 3300\,K, while all four
direct starts converge. Continuation therefore follows one additional sampled
point on the high-gravity cool-star branch, but it is not a general improvement
over direct initialization.

Formal convergence is not the same as a physically satisfactory atmosphere.
The continued \NMstarDwarfCoolestContinuation\,K dwarf has a maximum all-layer
flux imbalance of \NMstarDwarfFluxCoolest\%, compared with
\NMstarDwarfFluxWarm\% at 3750\,K. The retained M-giant atmospheres span
\NMstarGiantFluxMinimum--\NMstarGiantFluxMaximum\%. The cool-dwarf result
therefore demonstrates a numerically connected path, not a validated extension
of the atmosphere grid. Spectral comparisons are still absent, and these eight
solar-composition nodes do not establish general M-dwarf or M-giant support
below 4000\,K.

  \caption{Temperature and gravity dependence of the cool-star boundary test.
    The left column shows M dwarfs and the right column M giants. The upper

    reach the 30-iteration limit, and crosses mark temperatures not reached
    after an earlier failure in the sequence. The lower panels show the maximum
    all-layer flux imbalance for the retained atmosphere, using the temperature

    reaches the 3500\,K dwarf missed by the direct start, but the large flux
    residual prevents interpreting that point as a validated atmosphere.}
  \label{fig:mstar-solver}
\end{figure*}

\subsection{A learned two-field emulator}
\label{sec:learned}

We next test the complete two-field physical initializer rather than the
representation alone. Its network maps the five stellar labels to
$(\log_{10}m,\log_{10}T)$ on the optical-depth grid; the physical completion
then supplies the other four fields before the atmosphere iteration.

Column mass must increase monotonically with depth. We impose this condition
through the output parameterization. On the uniform $\log_{10}\tau$ grid, the
network predicts an anchor and positive increments,
\begin{equation}
  \ell_0 = a(\theta), \qquad
  \Delta\ell_j = \epsilon + \mathrm{softplus}\bigl(s_j(\theta)\bigr), \qquad
  \ell_j = \ell_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{j}\Delta\ell_k ,
  \label{eq:monotone}
\end{equation}
where $\ell_j=\log_{10}m_j$, $\epsilon=10^{-6}$\,dex per layer, and the
network predicts $a$ and $s_j$ from the stellar labels. The cumulative sum
guarantees a strictly increasing column-mass profile.

Two learned configurations enter the experiments. The development comparison
uses the \NnetDepth$\times$\NnetWidth\ monotone network directly. Before the
independent test, the same functional form was retrained with all development
and independent-test rows excluded and was augmented by two label-local
corrections. For standardized labels $\mathbf z$, each correction uses
radial-basis weights
\begin{equation}
  w_i(\mathbf z)=
  \exp\left[-\frac{\lVert\mathbf z-\mathbf c_i\rVert^2}{2\sigma^2}\right],
\end{equation}
and forms depth-dependent logarithmic offsets
$\delta_{T,j}=\sum_iw_i a^{T}_{ij}$ and
$\delta_{d,j}=\sum_iw_i a^{d}_{ij}$. If
$d_0=m_0$ and $d_j=m_j-m_{j-1}$, the corrected profiles are
\begin{equation}
  T'_j=T_j\,10^{\delta_{T,j}},\qquad
  d'_j=d_j\,10^{\delta_{d,j}},\qquad
  m'_j=\sum_{k=0}^{j}d'_k .
  \label{eq:rbf-correction}
\end{equation}
The weights are not normalized; the corrections therefore decay to zero away
from their centres rather than forming a partition of unity.
The first correction has three centres, $\sigma=0.30$, and offsets bounded by
$0.2$\,dex. Its loss is the mean squared logarithmic error in $T$ and $m$
after one differentiable solver iteration relative to the converged
six-field atmosphere, plus $0.05$ times the corresponding error of the
corrected initial profiles relative to the corpus atmosphere. The second has
20 centres and $\sigma=0.08$; these centres are the remaining profile
outliers in the development sample and a previously opened 200-star audit
sample. The independent 200-star sample was excluded from both corrections.
The base network, both corrections, the independent sample, and all
comparison rules were fixed before that sample was examined.

The two-field emulator is more accurate than the six-field network in the median
for the shared coordinates, although the comparison inverts in the tail: its
$p_{95}$ temperature error is
\NlearnedTempPfive\ against \NprodTempPfive, and $p_{95}$ column-mass error
\NlearnedMassPfive\,dex against \NprodMassPfive\,dex.

The more consequential comparison concerns the four fields the two-field
network never predicts. Table~\ref{tab:fields} compares three constructions
on the same development sample: six fields
predicted directly, learned $(m,T)$ followed by physical completion, and exact
$(m,T)$ followed by the same completion. Conditional on successful
reconstruction, the learned two-field path reduces the dependent-field
errors by factors of \NfieldGainLow\ to \NfieldGainHigh\ relative to direct
six-field prediction. The improvement arises from enforcing the equation of
state, opacity, radiative-transfer, and hydrostatic relations during
initialization.

\subsection{A hydrostatic grey--convective initializer}
\label{sec:vfour}

The learned experiment does not establish that an emulator is necessary. To
test that question directly, we construct $m(\tau)$ and $T(\tau)$ from the
stellar labels and physical approximations. The construction combines a grey
column-mass profile with a convectively adjusted temperature profile. It
first adopts the Eddington-grey relation
\citep{mihalas1978,hubeny2014}
\begin{equation}
  T_{\rm grey}^4(\tau)
  = \frac{3}{4} T_{\rm eff}^4\left(\tau+\frac{2}{3}\right)
\end{equation}
and integrates
\begin{equation}
  \frac{{\rm d}m_{\rm grey}}{{\rm d}\tau}
  = \frac{1}{\kappa_{\rm R}^{\rm app}
  (T_{\rm grey},P_{\rm grey})},
  \qquad P_{\rm grey}=g\,m_{\rm grey}.
\end{equation}
The approximate opacity is a Rosseland harmonic mean over fixed quadrature
nodes. It includes H$^-$ and H\,I bound-free and free-free absorption,
H$_2^+$ and He$^-$ continua, electron scattering, and H\,I Rayleigh
scattering; the electron density is obtained from Saha ionization of hydrogen
and the principal electron donors. Published threshold cross-sections are
used for the lowest H\,I levels in the cool branch. This opacity is used only
to construct the initial state; the atmosphere iteration subsequently uses
the solver's full opacity calculation.
A Saha-aware adiabatic adjustment then replaces the temperature in convective
layers \citep{bohmvitense1958}. The solver is initialized with
\begin{equation}
  m_{\rm seed}=m_{\rm grey},\qquad
  T_{\rm seed}=T_{\rm conv},\qquad
  \kappa_{\rm seed}=
  \kappa_{\rm R}^{\rm app}(T_{\rm conv},P_{\rm grey}).
  \label{eq:vfour-seed}
\end{equation}
The grey column mass is retained after the convective temperature adjustment;
it is not re-integrated with the modified temperature. All
\NphysicalDevFiniteSeeds\ development initial structures are finite and
positive, and the opacity
is recomputed consistently from $T_{\rm conv}$ and
$P_{\rm grey}=g\,m_{\rm grey}$. The construction contains
\NvfourFittedParameters\ fitted parameters and does not use the atmosphere
emulator.

On the development sample, the initializer converges for
\NphysicalDevConverged/\NphysicalDevStars\ stars within
\NphysicalIterationLimit\ iterations. Among successful calculations, the mean
is \NphysicalDevIterMean\ iterations, the median is
\NphysicalDevIterMedian, and the maximum is \NphysicalDevIterMax.
\NphysicalDevAboveFifteen\ successful stars require more than 15 iterations.
The remaining \NphysicalDevNotConverged\ stars do not converge within 60
iterations. Extending those same cases to
\NphysicalResidualIterations\ iterations does not recover any of them; all
\NphysicalResidualStars\ reach the \NphysicalResidualTimeoutSeconds-s limit.
On the \NphysicalDevCommon\ stars for which both the physical and six-field
starts converge, the corresponding mean costs are
\NphysicalDevCommonPhysicalMean\ and
\NphysicalDevCommonReferenceMean\ iterations, with a median physical-minus-
reference difference of \NphysicalDevCommonDifferenceMedian\ iterations.
Thus independence from the emulator is obtained at a substantial and
occasionally prohibitive increase in iteration cost.

To identify which part of the physical construction matters, we compare the
selected grey--convective start with a grey atmosphere and with a convective
construction that re-integrates column mass after changing the temperature.
The grey--convective start converges for
\NvfourDecoupledConverged/\NvfourMatchedStars\ stars, compared with
\NvfourGreyConverged/\NvfourMatchedStars\ for the grey start and
\NvfourConvectiveConverged/\NvfourMatchedStars\ for the coupled convective
start. Its gains relative to grey are $+\NvfourGainGreyAll$ stars overall and
$+\NvfourGainGreyCool$ cool stars. The improvement is therefore real but
uneven across label space. Retaining the grey mass coordinate is empirically
preferable in this comparison, although these convergence counts alone do not
identify the physical origin of the difference.

The physical seed is deliberately approximate. Its development-sample median
column-mass error is \NphysicalDevSeedMassMedian\,dex and its median
temperature error is \NphysicalDevSeedTempMedian. These offsets are visible
directly in the profile families of Fig.~\ref{fig:profiles}. They do not
prevent most stars from reaching the same atmosphere, but they explain the
longer contraction histories in Fig.~\ref{fig:convergence}.

Of the \NphysicalDevStars\ development stars,
\NphysicalDevSpectra\ have both a converged physical-start atmosphere and a
reference spectrum; \NphysicalDevSpectraExcluded\ do not enter the spectral
comparison. The median maximum normalized-flux difference is
\NphysicalDevSpectraMedian, and \NphysicalDevSpectraOver\ paired spectra exceed
the common \NgateBar\ reference level. The spectral distribution is
conditional on convergence and is therefore reported separately from the six
solver failures.

\subsection{Independent learned test and post-hoc physical comparison}
\label{sec:blind}

The learned model and both local corrections were fixed before the
independent 200-star sample was examined, and no subsequent result changed
their parameters. The learned initializer does not retain its development
profile or spectral accuracy on this sample (Fig.~\ref{fig:blind}). The
column-mass $p_{95}$ error more than doubles to \NblindMassPfive\,dex, and
\NblindUnionBlowouts\ stars develop large profile discrepancies
(Table~\ref{tab:blind}); \NblindSpecOver\ of the \NblindPaired\ paired spectra
exceed the common reference level.

The learned initializer nevertheless remains faster on the independent
sample: the paired calculations save \NblindPairedDiffMedian\ iterations in
the median, and the bootstrap 95 per cent interval for the mean saving is
\NblindPairedDiffCiLo\ to \NblindPairedDiffCiHi. The two local corrections
change only \NblindAdapterMovedMillidex/\NblindStars\ predictions by more than
$10^{-3}$\,dex, so the speed difference is primarily a property of the
underlying two-field network.

After the sample had been examined, we repeated the learned calculation with
the four dependent fields reconstructed solely from predicted $(m,T)$ and the
stellar labels. This removes any dependence on six-field emulator outputs at
inference while leaving the convergence and spectral conclusions essentially
unchanged (Table~\ref{tab:blind}). Because this reconstruction check was
performed after inspecting the sample, it is a post-hoc diagnostic rather
than a second independent test.

The hydrostatic grey--convective initializer was also developed after this
sample had been examined. Its formulae and numerical limits were fixed before
the calculation, and all 200 outcomes are retained. This tests whether the
development behavior extends across the same label distribution, but it is
not independent evidence.

The physical initializer produces finite, positive seeds for
\NphysicalPostFiniteSeeds/\NphysicalPostStars\ stars, but converges less often
and requires substantially more iterations than the six-field start
(Table~\ref{tab:physical_initializer}). The failure set---\NphysicalPostTimeouts\
timeouts and \NphysicalPostNotConverged\ calculation that exhausts the
iteration budget---is concentrated in temperature:
\NphysicalPostMidTempFailures\ of these \NphysicalPostFailureCount\ cases lie between
\NphysicalPostMidTempLow--\NphysicalPostMidTempHigh\,K, although this interval
contains only \NphysicalPostMidTempStars\ of the 200 stars. The failures show
no comparable concentration in $\log g$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:blind}c). This
temperature dependence is consistent with a limitation near the transition
from appreciable surface convection to predominantly radiative transport,
rather than with a cool-star or low-gravity boundary alone.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

The exact-coordinate experiment shows that $m(\tau)$ and $T(\tau)$ contain
the information needed to reconstruct the remaining stored atmospheric
profiles within the numerical precision relevant for the emergent spectrum.
At fixed stellar labels, the equation of state, opacity, radiative transfer,
and hydrostatic equilibrium constrain $P_{\rm gas}$, $n_{\rm e}$,
$\kappa_{\rm R}$, and $g_{\rm rad}$. Treating those four quantities as
independent coordinates is therefore unnecessary for this atmosphere family
and can introduce inconsistencies that the solver must remove.

Prediction is harder than representation. The learned two-field model reduces
the iteration count on both the development and independent samples, but its
profile and spectral errors have a pronounced independent-sample tail. The
two local radial-basis corrections affect only
\NblindAdapterMovedMillidex/\NblindStars\ independent predictions at the
$10^{-3}$-dex level; the measured speed improvement is therefore associated
mainly with the base two-field model. Faster convergence is not, by itself,
evidence of a more accurate final atmosphere. The predictor must be judged
through both the solver trajectory and the converged state \citep{um2020}.

The grey--convective calculation shows that a learned atmosphere is not
required to enter the solver basin for most sampled stars. Retaining
$m_{\rm grey}$ while applying the convective temperature adjustment gives the
highest convergence fraction among the three physical constructions tested.
The grey column mass carries the integrated opacity and hydrostatic scaling of
the initial atmosphere; re-integrating it after changing $T$ perturbs both
coordinates through the approximate opacity. Preserving $m_{\rm grey}$ may
therefore retain more of the original hydrostatic structure while the solver
adjusts the temperature. This interpretation is plausible but not established
by the convergence counts alone. The practical cost is clear: successful
development cases require \NphysicalDevIterMean\ iterations on average, and
failures persist even when the iteration budget is extended.

The cool-star experiment exposes the distinction between entering a numerical
convergence basin and obtaining an atmosphere in radiative--convective balance.
Within the eight solar-composition nodes, low-gravity giants are substantially
easier to initialize directly than high-gravity dwarfs. This contrast may
reflect the stronger coupling of molecular opacity, pressure, and convection
in the dense dwarf atmospheres, but the sparse grid cannot identify the
mechanism. The successful continuation to
\NMstarDwarfCoolestContinuation\,K nevertheless shows that neighbouring
solutions in the reduced coordinates can guide the solver where a direct
MARCS start fails. Its \NMstarDwarfFluxCoolest\% flux imbalance, and the failure
of the next temperature step, show equally clearly that reaching the
temperature stopping criterion is not enough. A flux-aware convergence test
and spectral validation are required before the low-temperature domain can be
extended.

The scope remains limited by the atmosphere corpus, which contains models
that originally converged in fewer than thirty iterations. The experiments do
not show that either initializer recovers regions where the reference method
fails. The targeted M-star calculation lies outside that corpus but covers only
eight solar-composition nodes and has no spectral validation. Solver iterations
also exclude the cost of constructing the initial state, and the spectral
comparison is restricted to
\NgateWindowLo--\NgateWindowHi\,nm. Finally, the 200-star physical comparison
was performed after that sample had been used for model testing, and the
spectral distributions are conditional on both atmospheres converging. These
results establish representational
sufficiency and expose the accuracy--cost trade-off; they do not yet establish
robustness for routine use.

The residual reconstruction error is concentrated near the upper boundary.
Appendix~\ref{app:resolution} shows that neither refinement of the interior
optical-depth grid nor denser quadrature removes this behavior, implicating
the approximation used above the first depth point. Atmospheres extending to
smaller optical depth are needed to determine whether a modified surface
boundary condition reduces this residual. For the physical initializer, the
next methodological step is to improve the approximate mass-column profile
while retaining an independent evaluation sample for subsequent testing.
\section{Conclusions}
\label{sec:conclusions}

Within the sampled stellar-label range, a converged 1D LTE atmosphere can be
represented by $m(\tau)$ and $T(\tau)$. Reconstructing the four dependent
profiles through the solver's physical closure reproduces both the atmospheric
structure and the emergent spectrum. The closure must be iterated at fixed
$(m,T)$ before the temperature correction begins.

A learned two-field initializer reduces the mean iteration count from
\NprodIterMean\ to \NlearnedIterMean\ and produces smoother convergence on
the development sample. The speed advantage persists on the independent
200-star sample, whereas the profile and spectral accuracy develop a
substantial tail. The representation is sufficient, but the present predictor
is not uniformly reliable across the sampled label range.

An emulator-independent grey--convective atmosphere initializes most sampled
stars successfully, but converged development cases require about
\NphysicalDevIterMean\ iterations on average and failures remain. A learned
atmosphere is therefore not physically necessary for initialization, but it
remains valuable for computational efficiency. The physical route requires an
independent evaluation before routine use.

Temperature continuation in the reduced coordinates reaches a
\NMstarDwarfCoolestContinuation\,K M dwarf for which direct initialization
fails. It does not yet extend the validated physical domain: the sequence fails
at the next cooler node, and the recovered atmosphere retains a
\NMstarDwarfFluxCoolest\% all-layer flux imbalance. This result motivates
continuation as a route into cool-star parameter space while requiring flux
balance and spectra before any claim of M-dwarf coverage.

\begin{appendix}

\section{Physical reconstruction algorithm}
\label{app:remat}

Given $m(\tau)$, $T(\tau)$, and labels $\theta$, the dependent profiles are
reconstructed on the grid of Eq.~(\ref{eq:grid}) as follows.

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \emph{Seed.} An atmosphere object is constructed carrying $m$ and $T$ on
    the optical-depth grid. The remaining fields are initialized from the labels and
    hydrostatic balance alone: $P_{\rm gas}=g\,m$, with positive $n_{\rm e}$
    and $\kappa_{\rm R}$ placeholders and $g_{\rm rad}=0$. The
    molecular equation of state and the first opacity and transfer passes
    overwrite these values. They therefore define only the starting point of
    the physical closure; no fields from the six-field model are used. A
    profile whose column mass is not strictly increasing is not physically
    admissible and is excluded.
  \item \emph{Populations.} The equation of state is solved for the chemical
    populations and the electron density at each layer.
  \item \emph{Opacity.} Continuum and line opacities are evaluated and combined
    into the Rosseland mean $\kappa_{\rm R}$.
  \item \emph{Transfer.} The radiative transfer solution supplies the radiation
    pressure and the radiative acceleration $g_{\rm rad}$.
  \item \emph{Closure.} The gas pressure is recomputed from
    Eq.~(\ref{eq:hse}) with the radiation-pressure term now known.
\end{enumerate}

Steps 2--5 form one closure iteration. They are repeated because the
populations and opacities in steps~2--3 use the pressure at the start of a
pass, while step~5 updates that pressure from the radiation field they imply.
The exact-coordinate calculations use \NsyncPasses\ fixed iterations. The
learned initializer uses at most \NsyncMaxPasses\ iterations and a
pressure-change tolerance of \NsyncPressureTolerance\,dex. Initial structures
that do not reach this tolerance are reported as reconstruction failures.
Neither $m$ nor $T$ is modified, and the depth grid is unchanged.

\section{Accuracy and convergence criteria}
\label{app:gates}

\emph{Profiles.} We calculate the pointwise relative error in temperature and
the pointwise absolute error in $\log_{10} m$ relative to the converged
atmosphere. A star is classified as having a large profile discrepancy if its
maximum temperature error exceeds $10$ percent or its maximum column-mass
error exceeds $0.1$\,dex.

\emph{Convergence.} The same atmosphere solver is initialized from each tested
state. We record the fraction of stars that converge; the
iteration count of the converging trial; the geometric mean of the ratio $q_k =
r_{k+1}/r_k$ of successive deep-layer temperature residuals; and the fraction of
trajectories on which $r_k$ is not monotonically decreasing. A state that
satisfies the temperature stopping rule but is not finite is counted as a
non-convergence.

\emph{Spectra.} Converged atmospheres from each pair of initial states are
synthesized over
\NgateWindowLo--\NgateWindowHi\,nm at $R = \NgateResolution$ in double
precision. Three quantities are compared: the maximum absolute difference in
normalized flux; the maximum absolute difference in total flux, divided by the
continuum; and the maximum relative difference in the continuum. The common
reference level is \NgateBar\ for each quantity. The reference-solver restart
comparison in Table~\ref{tab:spectral} provides its numerical scale; it is not
treated as a universal boundary between acceptable and unacceptable
atmospheres.

\section{Solver behavior by label sampling}
\label{app:baseline}

Table~\ref{tab:baseline} shows what the unmodified solver does when started
from the six-field initializer. The solver and the initializer are
identical in all four rows; only the way in which the stellar labels are drawn
changes, and the resulting spread is the point of the comparison. Drawing
labels uniformly across the label ranges the corpus spans gives
\NboxConverged\ convergence and \NboxFailed\ outright failures, whereas
resampling the corpus's own label distribution gives \NiidConverged\
convergence, with a $90$th-percentile iteration count of \NiidPninety. This
contrast quantifies the sensitivity of convergence statistics to the sampled
label distribution.

\input{tables/tab_baseline}

\section{Resolution and boundary controls}
\label{app:resolution}

The representation-resolution calculation maps converged $(m,T)$ curves
through intermediate optical-depth grids before physical reconstruction.
Increasing the intermediate grid from \NresCoarse\ to \NresFinest\ points
changes the median column-mass round-trip error from \NresCoarseError\ to
\NresFinestError, while the solver behavior remains near the three-iteration
floor. A separate quadrature control increases the integration density by a
factor of 16 while holding the surface seed fixed. Its top-layer $p_{99}$
residual changes only from \NcontinuityBasePninetyNine\ to
\NcontinuityRefinedPninetyNine\,dex, and the maximum from
\NcontinuityBaseMax\ to \NcontinuityRefinedMax\,dex. The remaining residual is
therefore associated with the upper boundary rather than the interior grid
spacing.

\section{Analytic initializer and additional comparisons}
\label{app:analytic}

The analytic initializer replaces the neural predictor with a low-rank formula
for a grey-normalized temperature residual and $\log_{10}\kappa_{\rm R}$.
Column mass is then obtained by integrating
${\rm d}m/{\rm d}\tau=1/\kappa_{\rm R}$. The formula is fitted to the same
atmosphere family but is evaluated only on the development sample. It provides
a compact fitted comparison for profile accuracy and convergence. The
hydrostatic grey--convective initializer provides the corresponding zero-fit
physical comparison on the same development stars.

\input{tables/tab_analytic_comparison}

The analytic formula contains \NanalyticConstants\ floating-point
coefficients and fixed constants, fitted on \NanalyticTrainStars\ atmospheres
and checked on \NanalyticValStars\ validation atmospheres. Its three
temperature regimes use complete cubic functions of the stellar labels and
five Chebyshev modes in depth. The formula is therefore much more compact than
the neural model, but it remains a fitted description of the same atmosphere
family.

The monotonic column-mass parameterization is also physically consequential.
On held-out atmospheres it gives $p_{95}$ errors of \NmonoTempPfive\ in
temperature and \NmonoMassPfive\,dex in column mass, with
\NmonoViolations\ non-monotonic profiles. Directly predicting all depth
points reduces these errors to \NdirectTempPfive\ and
\NdirectMassPfive\,dex, but produces \NdirectViolations\ inadmissible
column-mass profiles. We therefore retain the monotonic construction.
